textbookText: 6.3 Centripetal Acceleration Since there is a change in velocity in a circular motion, there is some acceleration present that is known by the name centripetal acceleration. The centripetal acceleration is the acceleration experienced by an object moving in a circular path. It is always directed towards the center of the circle along the radius and is responsible for keeping the object moving in its circular track. The magnitude of centripetal acceleration can be calculated using the formula: a = v2/r where v is the linear velocity of the object and r is the radius of the circular path. Let us consider a body of mass m undergoing a uniform circular motion in a circle of radius r and center at O. Initially, the body is at point A (t=0) that reaches to a point B in a small time Δt such that VA and VB are the velocities at the respective points and |VA| = |VB| = v. The angular displacement subtended at the center is θ.

Centripetal force is the force directed towards the center of a body undergoing uniform circular
motion. As we have derived an expression for centripetal acceleration, any object in circular
motion experiences a force directed towards the center to maintain uniform circular motion.

Fig 6.8: Showing centripetal force When we travel in a vehicle along a highway road with innumerable bends, we lean outward at every moment along the bends. On a circular track near the bends, the vehicle is subjected to a centripetal force, creating a similar sensation on the lower part of our body in contact with the vehicle. The upper part, therefore, leans outwards in opposition to this force, which is compensated for by the centrifugal force.
While undergoing a circular path, a body experiences centrifugal force, given by F=mrω2 For a longer string, r increases, thereby requiring more force to maintain the circular motion.
